## Focus Question

**How did culture history bring order to the archaeological record, and which parts of its framework should archaeologists retain or reject today?**

Urban and Schortman (2019) show how culture history organized archaeological materials through typology, chronology, and space-time systematics. They also show how concepts such as “culture,” “boundary,” and “periphery” shaped what archaeologists expected to find.

Feinman and Neitzel (2020) accept the need for chronology and spatial ordering but reject the assumptions built into culture-historical units: **biological-cultural correspondence, homogeneity, discrete boundaries, primordial identity, and sudden collective change.**

Choose one pathway and write a **one-page, single-spaced reflection**.

## Pathway A — GenAI Critical Evaluation

Ask GenAI whether culture history is still useful in archaeology.

Evaluate its answer against the readings and lecture, identifying what should be retained and what should be rejected.

## Pathway B — Scholarly Critical Comparison

Compare Urban and Schortman (2019) with Feinman and Neitzel (2020) on the value and limits of culture history.

Consider whether archaeological “cultures” are useful analytical tools or whether they risk turning variable, overlapping social relations into bounded groups.

## Conclusion

Conclude with **your own position**, supported by specific examples from the readings.

## Required Readings

Urban, Patricia and Edward Schortman. 2019. *Archaeological Theory in Practice*. Routledge, Abingdon. Chapter 3, [“Culture History”](https://go.exlibris.link/g0Q5DM0g), pp. 41–72.

Feinman, Gary M., and Jill E. Neitzel. 2020. [“Excising Culture History from Contemporary Archaeology.”](https://go.exlibris.link/g9N46lzz) *Journal of Anthropological Archaeology* 60:101230.
